title: Derby, Colorado well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Around Derby, median well depth is 35 ft and median yield is 30 gpm. See what that means for drilling cost and water supply on your property.
h1: Water well depths and costs around Derby, Colorado
intro_html: Derby sits on the plains in Adams County, where wells tap mostly shallow alluvial and Denver Basin sedimentary formations. Within 5 miles there are 8,934 well permits on record, so we have a good picture of how deep wells run, how much water they produce, and what they typically cost. This page walks through what the local data means if you are buying or building on a property served by a well near Derby or nearby areas like Welby, North Washington, or Henderson.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in the Derby area
sections.html: Within 5 miles of Derby, reported well depths are generally shallow compared to much of Colorado. The median total depth is 35 feet, and the middle half of wells fall between 22 and 50 feet. About 89% of wells are under 100 feet. Only 3% are 100–300 feet, 5% reach 300–600 feet, and 3% go deeper than 600 feet. The deepest well on record is 1,626 feet, likely a deep Denver Basin well drilled for a specific purpose, not the norm for homes. For a typical domestic or small irrigation well around Derby, drillers usually plan shallow casing into alluvial or unnamed/fractured-bedrock aquifers, with deeper Denver aquifers reserved for particular needs or regulated uses.

sections.heading: Water levels and long-term trend under Derby
sections.html: Static water levels around Derby are quite shallow. The median depth to water is 9 feet, with the middle half of measurements between 6 and 22 feet below the surface. Looking at trends by decade, the median was about 30 feet in the 1960s, then 21 feet in the 2000s, 9 feet in the 2010s, and 8 feet so far in the 2020s. That series does not show a dropping water table in this dataset; if anything, measured water levels have become shallower over time. Most wells here are in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers (6,485 wells) and alluvial deposits (1,087 wells), with 162 wells specifically marked as Denver aquifer. Even with generally shallow water, each parcel can vary, so always check nearby well logs before designing foundation drains, basements, or septic.

sections.heading: How much water Derby wells typically produce
sections.html: Of the wells that report pump testing around Derby, production is generally strong. The median reported yield is 30.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half of wells fall between 14.0 and 200.0 gpm. None of the reported wells are under 1 gpm, and only 1% fall in the 1–5 gpm range. About 24% produce 5–15 gpm, and 75% are 15+ gpm. For a single household on an exempt well, 5–10 gpm is usually adequate; many Derby-area wells exceed that. Keep in mind this is test data from 232 wells, not every permit. Individual yields still depend on the specific aquifer (alluvial vs deeper Denver) and how the well is completed, so a new well should still be test-pumped and measured.

sections.heading: Who is drilling around Derby and when
sections.html: Derby’s well history is long and active. Permits pick up from 358 in the 1950s and 365 in the 1960s, then 202 in the 1970s as development patterns shifted. Activity rises again in the 1980s with 627 permits and jumps in the 1990s to 1,460. The 2000s saw 1,229 permits, and the 2010s are busiest so far with 2,205. There are already 716 permits in the 2020s, with the newest in 2025, so well work is ongoing. This mix is dominated by monitoring wells (about 62%), with domestic/household use around 15%, irrigation 5%, and stock 1%. Major drillers in the records include Authorized (Pe, Pg) with 2,457 wells, Layne, Christensen Co. (Tormoehlen, David A.) with 188, and Boyles Bros. Drilling Co. (Lensch, George E) with 156.

sections.heading: Expected cost to drill a new well near Derby
sections.html: Ground here is Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock with shallow alluvial cover in places, and local drilling runs about $50–$70 per foot. At the median total depth of 35 feet, the drilled hole alone pencils out around $1,800–$2,400. Once you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical tie-in, a typical complete well system in this depth range runs roughly $7,800–$14,400. If your design or water court situation pushes you to a few hundred feet into a Denver aquifer instead of the shallow alluvium, the per-foot rate is similar but the total cost scales up quickly with depth, so it is important to look at nearby logs and your intended use before you budget.

sections.heading: Local risks: contamination, low yield, and site layout
sections.html: From a production standpoint, the Derby area data do not show many weak wells: 0% of reported yields are under 1 gpm and only 1% are 1–5 gpm. The main caution here is water quality. Within about 10 miles there are 645 mapped PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 171 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites, plus a historic mine feature. That does not mean your well is contaminated, but it does mean you should plan on full lab testing for PFAS and other contaminants before relying on a well for drinking. With shallow water tables (median 9 feet), careful septic placement and grading are also important to keep wastewater separated from your well.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot with a well near Derby
sections.html: If you are buying in Derby, Welby, North Washington, Henderson, or nearby, start by pulling the DWR permit and completion log for the specific well. Compare its total depth to the local median of 35 feet and see where its static water level sits relative to the 6–22 foot middle range. Ask for any pump test showing yield; in this area you should be comfortable if you see something in the teens or higher, given the 30.0 gpm median. On vacant land, check whether you can drill a standard exempt household well or need augmentation. Finally, budget based on the local cost range and plan to test water quality thoroughly, especially given the number of mapped PFAS and cleanup sites in the broader area.

faq.q: How deep are water wells around Derby, Colorado?
faq.a: In the Derby area, the median reported well depth is 35 feet, with the middle half of wells between 22 and 50 feet deep. About 89% of wells are under 100 feet, and only a small share reach into the hundreds of feet. The deepest well on record is 1,626 feet, but that is an outlier; most domestic wells are relatively shallow compared to other parts of Colorado.

faq.q: How much water do Derby, CO wells typically produce?
faq.a: Reported pump tests near Derby show a median yield of 30.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 14.0 and 200.0 gpm. None of the reported wells are under 1 gpm, and only about 1% fall in the 1–5 gpm range. Around 24% produce 5–15 gpm and 75% are 15+ gpm, which is more than enough for typical household use when combined with proper storage and pressure equipment.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a water well in Derby, Colorado?
faq.a: Local drilling in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock runs about $50–$70 per foot. At the area’s median depth of 35 feet, drilling alone is roughly $1,800–$2,400. A complete well system with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical typically totals in the $7,800–$14,400 range at this depth. Deeper Denver aquifer wells cost more because the per-foot rate applies over a greater total depth.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink near Derby, CO?
faq.a: Water safety depends on the specific well. Within about 10 miles of Derby there are 645 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 171 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, plus a historic mine feature. Those are regional indicators, not a direct test of any one well. If you are buying or drilling in this area, plan on a full laboratory water analysis, including PFAS and common inorganics, before using the water for drinking.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping in wells around Derby, Colorado?
faq.a: The available static water level data do not show a long-term decline in this area. Median depth to water was about 30 feet in the 1960s, 21 feet in the 2000s, 9 feet in the 2010s, and 8 feet so far in the 2020s. Overall, measured water levels have been relatively shallow, with a current median of 9 feet and most readings between 6 and 22 feet below the ground surface.
